newsitem.title: USA: Trade worries weigh on dollar after new high vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Trade worries weigh on dollar after new high vs mark.

text.p: The dollar extended its string of gains to a new 34-month high against the mark on Wednesday but ended lower after signs of trade troubles with Japan and fears of higher Japanese interest rates bolstered the yen.

The dollar touched 1.7169 marks in Asia, its strongest since late April 1994. But the rally sputtered as the U.S. currency turned sharply lower against the yen after a report showed Japan's trade surplus jumped in February and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the United States was very "watchful" of its trade deficit with Japan.

"Rubin made a few comments overnight and the Japanese trade number came out showing an increase in the surplus and of course that has helped the yen," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
The dollar ended at 121.15 yen, down from 122.15 yen late Tuesday.
Japan's overall trade surplus swelled more than 53 percent to 197.33 billion yen in the first 20 days of February, compared with one year ago.

The yen tends to strengthen when Japan's trade surplus grows because the market believes the recent weakness of the Japanese currency, especially against the dollar, has given Japan an undeserved advantage in exporting its goods.

The yen also surged to its highest level against the mark since last June, getting an addional boost after Japan's chief government spokesman told a parliamentary committee that Japan needs to consider measures to deal with the adverse impact of low interest rates on incomes.

"Also last night a government spokesman from Japan was talking about being worried about interest rates, so there were a couple of reasons for people to perhaps buy back some yen here," said Keith Woodfin, currency analyst at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
With yields on Japanese financial instruments among the lowest in the world, pensioners in particular have lobbied the goverment hard to improve the returns on their retirement savings, Woodfin said.
The specter of higher Japanese interest rates increased the relative attractiveness of yen-denominated investments and made investors hesitant to buy dollars for yen, traders said.
But against the mark, interest rate differences should continue to favour the dollar because German interest rates are expected to remain low, while U.S. rates could increase, they added.

Financial markets were looking for more clues about U.S. interest rates from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who completed his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on the U.S. economy and interest rate outlook before the U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday.

The markets were upbeat after Greenspan's comments, which were a close replay of his address last week when he told a Senate panel the Fed could tighten credit even before solid signs of inflation emerge.

The dollar settled at 1.7127 marks, slightly below Tuesday's 1.7137 marks, but traders said it garnered support from strong Wall Street stocks. The Dow Jones industrial average gained more than 93 points to end at 6,945.85.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4815 Swiss francs from 1.4865 on Tuesday and to Canadian $1.3692 from C$1.3696. The pound rose to $1.6155 from $1.6138.
